## Critics of the multiverse {#the-multiverse-has-its-critics .smaller}

::: {.small}
- "Robustness is better assessed with a **few thoughtful models** than with billions of regressions" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed; answering @GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources] – only *justified* models targeting the *same estimand* belong in one curve. Our curve keeps the **`r fmt_n(nrow(spec_curve))`** specifications that an audit of every option judged justifiable for this claim, and a decomposition by fork does the job that every critic endorses: it locates where the argument must happen
- "**There is only one correct analysis**" once the question is fully specified [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne] – your preregistered specification guards against *cherry-picking*, and their deeper point is that preregistering a choice does not yet make it *justified*, which is what the estimand and DAG work were for
- "What's a multiverse **good for** anyway?" – reflection, persuasion, or inference, and each purpose needs a *differently built* universe [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood]. Our full menu serves **reflection** and the audited curve moves towards **persuasion**; how much more to read into it is the open debate
:::

::: {.src}
The book-length how-to: @YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational; the estimand diagnosis of the red-card study: @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
The method you practised is the subject of a live debate, and you can now read that debate for yourself. Katrin Auspurg, who with Josef Brüderl traced the spread in the red-card study to teams answering different questions, answered a 3.6-billion-estimate study with the line at the top of this slide: only thoughtful, justified models belong in a curve. Our own curve is built the way she recommends. Every option of the menu was audited for whether it is a justifiable answer to this claim, the curve keeps eight hundred and sixty-four specifications rather than an enumeration, and decomposing it by fork does the one job that every critic endorses, which is to show where the argument has to happen. Lakens and colleagues say that once the question is fixed, only one analysis implements it correctly. A preregistered specification guards against cherry-picking. Their deeper point, that preregistering a choice does not make it justified, is why the DAG comes before the preregistration. And Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman ask what a multiverse is for: reflection, persuasion, or inference, each needing a differently built set. Our full menu serves reflection, and the audited curve, with a published reason for every option, moves towards persuasion; how much more can be read into it is the open question in the debate you have now joined. [advance]
:::

## Identifying the one correct analysis {#how-would-you-know .smaller}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
On the red cards, twenty-nine teams modelled one count as **linear, logistic or Poisson**: claims about how the outcome was generated that cannot all be right, so on the argument of Lakens and colleagues most of that spread is error.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Grant the argument, and suppose that **one correct analysis exists**. Which one is it?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Getting there needs the estimand *and* the identification assumptions *and* agreement about the measurement – and on this claim, reasonable people disagree about all three.
:::

::: {.fragment}
So the curve complements the one-correct-analysis view: it is a **map of the disagreement that remains**, drawn because we cannot yet settle it.
:::

::: {.fragment}
And it points at what to argue about: on this claim, at the **estimator** – whether the comparison removes what all member states shared in a year – and at the **predictor**.
:::
::::

::: {.src}
@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne
:::

::: notes
Lakens and colleagues argue that a research question, once fully specified, implies one analysis that estimates its quantity, so that a spread of results is evidence that most of the specifications are wrong rather than of legitimate diversity. Take it back to the red cards, where twenty-nine teams modelled one count as linear, logistic or Poisson, claims about how the outcome was generated that cannot all be right, so that on the reading of Lakens and colleagues most of the spread is error, and I think the argument is largely right. So let us grant the argument. Suppose one correct analysis does exist. The next question is which one it is, and how you would know. To get there you need the estimand, and the identification assumptions, and agreement about how the construct is measured – and on this claim reasonable people disagree about all three, as you found for yourselves in the hands-on tasks. So I read the curve as a companion to the one-correct-analysis view rather than a rival to it. It is a map of the disagreement that remains, drawn because we cannot yet settle it. Read that way it is useful, because it shows where the disagreement is. On this claim it is at the estimator, which here is the choice between two questions, change in a country against the common European path or all change within a country, and at the predictor, unemployment or growth. Those are arguments about the claim itself, and they belong in the paper.
:::

## What preregistration settles {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**It does settle**

- That your specification was not chosen *because of* the result
- That your rule for what counts as support was fixed before you had a result
- That a reader can see what you intended, and what you changed
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**It does not settle**

- Whether the specification was **any good**
- Whether it estimates the quantity that your question implies
- Whether the assumptions behind it hold

A badly reasoned analysis that is preregistered is still badly reasoned; the preregistration only adds a timestamp
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
That is why the estimand and the DAG came **first** today: preregistration protects a choice, and the causal reasoning is what justifies it.
:::

::: notes
So where does preregistration fit? It settles a specific and limited set of things, and the two columns matter equally. On the left: it settles that your specification was not chosen because of the result it gave, that your rule for what counts as support was fixed before you had a result to bend it around, and that a reader can see both what you intended and what you subsequently changed. Those are real guarantees and no other mechanism provides them. On the right, what it does not settle: whether the specification was any good, whether it estimates the quantity that your question implies, or whether its assumptions hold. A badly reasoned analysis that is preregistered is still badly reasoned, only now with a timestamp on it. That is why we did the estimand and the graph first. Preregistration protects a choice, and the causal reasoning is what justifies it.
:::
